submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective detector of the fused dot-field token of an attribute access: the pole fires on the single tokenizer token that joins a period to a field name (`.value`, `.data`, `.child`, `.size`, `.timeout`, `.email`) in source code and in ordinary prose alike, reaching 0.4-0.8 in both (`cfg.timeout`, but also `She wrote sample.value on the board`). The fusion, not the code syntax or the sentence meaning, carries the signal: the same field word as a separate token after a space (`cfg timeout`, `sample value`) stays at the floor (0.14-0.29), and the field word modulates strength (`.child`, `.value`, `.data`, `.email` strong; `.id`, `.status` weak).

top_examples.text:
Q:

Google Big Query check if json key exists

I have a Google Big Query Table column, which contains a json string. Over time, new keys were introduced to this json string. 
time              col_b     
--------------------------------------------------
timestamp3        {"key1": "value", "key2": "value"}
timestamp2        {"key1": "value"}
timestamp1        {"key1": "value"}

How can I extract key2 and in case it doesn't exist fill with NaN?
I thought about something like:
SELECT 
    JSON_EXTRACT(col_b, "$.key2) AS key2
FROM db;

Doing this will throw the error, so it thinks it should be a double instead of a string cause of the null values. 
Bad double type: value

How can I check in advance whether key2 is existing and if not fill with null?

A:

See below example    
#standardSQL
WITH `project.dataset.table` AS (
  SELECT 'timestamp3' time, '{"key1": "value", "key2": "value"}' col_b UNION ALL
  SELECT 'timestamp2', '{"key1": "value"}' UNION ALL
  SELECT 'timestamp1', '{"key1": "value"}' 
)
SELECT *, IFNULL(JSON_EXTRACT_SCALAR(col_b, '$.key2'), 'NaN') AS key2
FROM `project.dataset.table`

with output    
Row time        col_b                               key2     
1   timestamp3  {"key1": "value", "key2": "value"}  value    
2   timestamp2  {"key1": "value"}                   NaN  
3   timestamp1  {"key1": "value"}                   NaN

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
On the first morning of the migration, the team gathered in a narrow room with two whiteboards and a projector that refused to turn on. They had spent three weeks cataloguing every field the old system had ever written, and now they needed to move those records without losing a single row. The lead engineer, a quiet woman named Mara, divided the work into four tracks: export, validation, replay and rollback. Each track had its own checklist, and every checklist ended with the same warning: never trust a schema you have not read yourself.

The export track was the simplest on paper. A small script walked the archive, opened each record in turn, and wrote a line of text for every field it found. The script had been written years earlier by an intern who no longer worked at the company, and nobody fully understood why it sorted the fields in reverse alphabetical order. Mara decided to leave that behavior alone. Changing it, she argued, would create more noise than the ordering itself, and noise was the enemy of a clean comparison.

Validation proved harder. The old records had been edited by dozens of people over a decade, and the edits had not always followed the rules. Some lines contained extra spaces. Some fields appeared twice with different spellings. A few records contained nothing at all beyond a timestamp and a name. The team built a checker that flagged every anomaly it could describe, then reviewed the flagged lines by hand, one folder at a time, until the pile of exceptions shrank to something they could carry into the next meeting.

Replay was the track everyone feared. During replay, the team fed the old records back into the new system and watched for differences. The first run produced four hundred mismatches, most of them trivial, a handful alarming. Mara printed the alarming ones and pinned them to the wall. The rollback plan stayed on a single page, taped beside the door, in case the replay broke something that could not be repaired quickly.

By the end of the second week the team had settled into a rhythm. They met at eight, argued until ten, wrote code until lunch, and tested until the light outside turned orange. On Thursday, when the loader reached the nested node, it read schema.child and stored the pointer in a table beside the original record. Nobody celebrated. The final sentence of the checklist still applied, and the rollback page still hung by the door.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Fused `schema.child` buried deep in a long narrative tests the retrospective detector at long distance and in prose, so the hypothesis predicts activation.
